segments.title: How a guard ship combined reserve readiness and port defence
segments.summary: Guard ships kept a partly crewed, fully stored warship ready at an important port while also serving as the local commander's headquarters and defensive reserve.
segments.body: A guard ship was a form of naval reserve assigned to an important port, commonly using a third-rate or fourth-rate ship of the line. A first-rate or second-rate could serve at an exceptionally critical port, though this was rare. The vessel remained fully stored but carried only a fraction of its wartime crew, enough to maintain it and provide the core around which a full crew could rapidly form. The ship also supported the port's defences and often housed the port admiral or captain and their staff. Making the vessel the commander's own flagship tied administrative authority directly to its material condition and created a strong incentive to keep it seaworthy.

evidence.note: Defines the guard ship as a partly crewed, fully stored port reserve and explains its command and maintenance roles.

segments.title: What quarter, half, and two-thirds crews could do
segments.summary: Crew fractions translated into distinct combat capabilities, from manning one gun deck to firing a broadside or combining gunnery with limited sailing.
segments.body: The apparent readiness of a fully rigged guard ship concealed how much its actual capability depended on manning. One-quarter was the normal peacetime floor, while a wartime guard ship might carry one-half to two-thirds of its crew. A quarter crew could maintain the ship and operate roughly one gun deck, while half a crew could produce a full broadside but could not simultaneously handle the sails. At roughly two-thirds or three-quarters strength, the ship could combine most of its gunnery with basic manoeuvring. Ports could therefore increase security incrementally by raising crew levels without fully commissioning a ship for general deployment.

evidence.note: Relates quarter, half, and higher crew complements to gun-deck operation, broadsides, sailing, and deployment status.

segments.title: Why a port might keep two partly crewed guard ships
segments.summary: Two fully rigged but partly crewed guard ships preserved a dependable local reserve and made it harder for an attacker to judge the port's true readiness.
segments.body: Fully crewing a guard ship made it an attractive candidate for deployment elsewhere, undermining its local purpose. A port could instead spread the same half-crew across two quarter-crewed vessels and retain two fully rigged, fully stored hulls. To an observer, those ships looked commissioned, making it difficult to tell whether the harbour contained guard ships, active warships, or one of each. That uncertainty strengthened port defence while preserving two reserve nuclei that could receive more sailors in an emergency.

evidence.note: Explains why two quarter-crewed ships provided more durable port security and greater uncertainty for an attacker than one fully crewed ship.

segments.title: How guard squadrons differed and what mobilising one cost
segments.summary: British ports usually relied on third rates while Dutch and other navies could use more fourth rates, but mobilising a whole guard squadron removed the port's own reserve protection.
segments.body: At major bases, guard-ship practice could scale into a squadron of eight, nine, or ten ships of the line. British formations usually relied on third rates because those vessels were numerous, whereas Dutch and other navies could make greater use of fourth rates; Britain often kept its fourth rates for distant peacetime stations. A vice-admiral of the port might command the force, with a rear-admiral and perhaps a commodore dividing it into subordinate groups. With roughly one-third crews, the ships could be made ready rapidly. Mobilising the entire formation created a direct trade-off because the port would lose the warships assigned to its own protection.

evidence.note: Compares British and Dutch guard-squadron composition, describes the flag-officer structure, and explains the cost of mobilising the port's whole reserve.

segments.title: Why hulks and ships in great refit were unavailable
segments.summary: Hulked vessels had become stationary facilities, while ships in great refit were being rebuilt too extensively to count as an available reserve.
segments.body: Readiness categories distinguished usable reserve ships from vessels that could not respond to an emergency. A hulk was not prepared to sail and might instead serve as a store ship, prison ship, or other stationary facility. A ship in great refit was being rebuilt from the keel upward and was likewise unavailable. Enough of the old vessel might remain for the work to retain the name of a refit, but its readiness resembled a new construction project. Both categories therefore sat far below the partly crewed guard ship in practical mobilization value.

evidence.note: Defines non-available ships as hulks or vessels in great refit and describes the condition and uses of each category.

segments.title: When a commissioned warship counted as a transport or store ship
segments.summary: Ships of the line could be commissioned for logistics rather than combat, carrying reduced armament to make room for troops or expedition supplies.
segments.body: A warship used as a troop transport or store ship occupied an unusual readiness category: it was commissioned, but not as a full fighting ship. Armed en flûte, it might retain only enough guns for one side, with guns shifted as circumstances required. Other vessels could land all their cannon to free displacement for troops or stores. Fleet totals can therefore be misleading when many nominal warships are serving the transport and supply system of an amphibious expedition.

evidence.note: Describes armed-en-flute troop and store ships and distinguishes their logistical commissions from full warship readiness.

segments.title: From ships in ordinary to guard ships ready within hours
segments.summary: A ship in ordinary needed refit, stores, crew, and work-up, whereas a fully stored guard ship retained the specialists needed for rapid mobilization.
segments.body: Ships in ordinary had no stores or crew and were often laid up in fresh water to preserve their hulls. When one returned to service, dockyard workers first inspected the hull and repaired the effects of a long voyage, a commission, or the time spent in ordinary. The vessel then required stores, recruitment, and a period of work-up, making readiness a matter of weeks or months. Guard ships occupied the immediately available tier: fully stored, minimally crewed, and carrying key officers and craftsmen. If enough sailors could be found locally, that nucleus could bring the ship toward sea readiness in hours rather than months.

evidence.note: Contrasts the weeks or months required for ships in ordinary with the stored and specialist-manned guard-ship nucleus.

segments.title: Edward Vernon mobilizes guard ships before war is declared
segments.summary: Vernon drew guard ships from two important ports to assemble a small force that reached the Caribbean almost as soon as the War of Jenkins' Ear began.
segments.body: Edward Vernon argued that a small fleet mobilized quickly at the opening of a war could achieve results unavailable to a larger but slower force. He assembled roughly eight vessels, including six fighting ships and two used in support roles, by taking guard ships from two critical ports. The force included two 70-gun ships, three 60-gun ships, and a 50-gun ship. Beginning the movement before the formal declaration of war allowed Vernon to appear off Portobelo in November 1739 before Spanish preparations caught up.

evidence.note: Connects Vernon's small early-deployed force and its ships to guard-ship mobilization at the start of the War of Jenkins' Ear.

segments.title: How Vernon's fleet captured Portobelo in 1739
segments.summary: The rapidly deployed Royal Navy force overwhelmed Portobelo's undermanned forts, captured prizes, wrecked the base, and withdrew at very low cost.
segments.body: Portobelo was an important staging point for the Spanish treasure system and possessed forts and troops even in peacetime, but its defences were not ready for Vernon's sudden arrival. An easterly wind forced the British ships toward the principal harbour fort, while sailors and Royal Marines landed, scaled its walls, lowered the Spanish colours, and raised the Royal Navy ensign. Although that fort supposedly had a 300-man garrison, only about 40 troops remained when it surrendered; the attackers then moved against Santiago Fortress and sank a Spanish sloop. The governor sought terms by the following day, and the British occupied Portobelo for three weeks while destroying its value as a maritime base. They took three prizes, including a snow renamed Triumph and two coastguard vessels, at a cost of three killed and seven wounded in the account presented here.

evidence.note: Narrates the approach, assault, surrender, casualties, prizes, occupation, and demolition at Portobelo.

segments.title: Deployment speed can matter more than fleet size
segments.summary: Guard ships let Vernon act with a smaller force before Spanish reinforcements arrived, demonstrating how readiness can overturn an opponent's planning timetable.
segments.body: Speed of deployment can place a force where an opponent does not yet expect it and inside the timetable on which their defences depend. Rapid forces may be numerically small, so their individual fighting power matters, but immediate availability can compensate for numbers. Vernon accepted perhaps a quarter of the fleet he might have assembled from ships in ordinary because waiting for those ships would have taken months. The smaller guard-ship force reached Portobelo before reinforcement, destroyed the base, and departed before Spain could respond effectively.

evidence.note: Draws the operational lesson that immediate availability enabled a smaller force to act before the Spanish timetable caught up.

segments.title: What guard ship means in the modern Royal Navy
segments.summary: Modern British guard ships are fully crewed patrol or combat vessels, including HMS Forth in the Falklands and frigates protecting the strategic deterrent.
segments.body: The modern British term no longer describes a ship held at quarter crew. In the Falklands, HMS Forth, a Batch 2 River-class offshore patrol vessel, performs presence, flag-showing, and coastguard-like duties comparable to older sloops. Its stationing also makes it a tripwire force even though the vessel is not intended to serve as a full combat warship. The name is also applied to the anti-submarine warfare ship that protects the strategic deterrent as submarines enter or leave port, commonly a Type 23 frigate in the period discussed. Russian usage applies the term to patrol boats, illustrating that the modern label does not identify one standard type of vessel. Across many navies, peacetime functions once associated with guard ships have instead moved to coastguards and patrol forces.

evidence.note: Contrasts historical partial-crew guard ships with modern British and Russian patrol, deterrent-protection, and coastguard roles.

segments.title: Reserve ships freed first-line forces for the decisive theatre
segments.summary: Older reserve and guard ships could cover trade protection and secondary theatres while modern first-line vessels concentrated where war made them most valuable.
segments.body: The guard-ship principle endured because a small standing nucleus could rapidly absorb reservists and other available sailors. By the eve of the First World War, older ships held in reserve were often unsuitable for the primary theatre but still valuable in secondary or tertiary duties. Mobilizing them allowed the navy's best peacetime ships to concentrate in the decisive theatre without abandoning trade protection, presence, and risk management elsewhere. Naval treaty limits later made it harder to retain large pools of older hulls for this purpose.

evidence.note: Explains the reserve nucleus, older ships' secondary-theatre role, concentration of prime vessels, and treaty-era constraints.

segments.title: Why modern navies still need reserves for long wars
segments.summary: Planning around short wars is hazardous because peer conflicts routinely outlast expectations, making ships, personnel, and mobilization infrastructure essential reserves.
segments.body: The historical guard-ship system points toward a broader modern problem: navies need credible reserves and a plan for expanding them. Strategies that assume a peer or near-peer war will be short have repeatedly disappointed their authors. Technological superiority alone cannot guarantee a quick decision; the supporting infrastructure must also be able to mobilize, sustain, and replace forces. A long-war posture therefore depends on both reserve assets and the institutional capacity to make them useful.

evidence.note: Argues for modern reserve planning and warns that peer wars commonly outlast short-war assumptions.
